intro.html: Too much can be too much of a thing (a surfeit of candy), too much in a price (exorbitant), too much for the job (superfluous), or too much in amount (excessive, inordinate). Some of these words also carry the idea of not needed or not belonging.

Too much in amount: excessive, inordinate, a surfeit, to inundate. Extra, left over: a surplus. Not needed: superfluous, redundant (repeated), gratuitous (uncalled for). Not belonging: extraneous. Too high a price: exorbitant.

Look for “over” and “out” inside them: super/sur (over) in superfluous, surplus and surfeit; ex and extra (out, outside) in excessive, exorbitant and extraneous; and the Latin unda (wave) in both inundate and redundant.

words.def: more than is necessary, normal or reasonable
words.ex: Ten straight minutes of honking seemed a bit {excessive}.
words.ctx: The fine of five hundred dollars for an overdue library book struck everyone as {excessive}; it was far more than the book itself was worth.
words.etym: From excess, from Latin excedere (to go beyond): ex- (out) + cedere (to go).

mn.text: Pip pours syrup on his pancakes until it floods the plate, drips off the table and puddles on the floor: the amount is {excessive}.

scene.alt: A boy pours so much syrup on his pancakes that it drips onto the floor while a woman gasps.

words.def: an amount left over beyond what is needed
words.ex: The bakery gave its {surplus} bread to the shelter each evening.
words.ctx: Because the farm grew far more corn than it could sell, it sent the {surplus} to a neighboring town that had suffered a poor harvest.
words.etym: From Old French surplus: sur (over) + plus (more).

mn.text: Nell’s garden grows so many watermelons that she sets the extras by the road with a FREE sign: they are her {surplus}.

scene.alt: A woman offers free watermelons from a big pile of extras by the road.

words.ex: With the sun shining all day, the umbrella turned out to be {superfluous}.
words.ctx: The editor cut every {superfluous} word from the article, so that the final version said just as much in half the space.
words.etym: From Latin superfluus, “overflowing”: super (over) + fluere (to flow).

mn.text: The snowman already has a carrot nose, but Pip keeps adding more until there are five: four of them are {superfluous}.

scene.alt: A boy sticks yet another carrot nose onto a snowman that already has four.

words.def: unnecessary because it repeats something already there
words.ex: “Free gift” is {redundant}, since every gift is free.
words.ctx: Once the town built a new bridge, the old ferry became {redundant}; there was no longer any need for a boat to carry people across.
words.etym: From Latin redundare, “to overflow”: re- (again) + undare (to rise in waves).

mn.text: The shop sign shouts, “FREE GIFT! NO CHARGE! COSTS NOTHING!” Saying the same thing three times is {redundant}.

scene.alt: A boy scratches his head at a shop banner that says the same thing twice: free gift, no charge.

words.def: not belonging; unrelated to the matter at hand
words.ex: Remove any {extraneous} details from your summary.
words.ctx: The detective ignored the {extraneous} gossip about the neighbor’s new car and focused only on the facts that bore on the missing painting.
words.etym: From Latin extraneus, “from outside,” from extra (outside).

mn.cue: EXTRA-neous: EXTRA stuff that doesn’t belong
mn.text: Pip’s poster about bees has a slice of pizza glued right in the middle: it has nothing to do with bees. The pizza is {extraneous}.

scene.alt: A teacher points at a slice of pizza stuck in the middle of a boy’s poster about bees.

words.def: far too high, especially of a price
words.ex: The airport charged an {exorbitant} price for a bottle of water.
words.ctx: Though the concert was wonderful, many fans stayed home because of the {exorbitant} ticket prices, which had doubled since the year before.
words.etym: From Late Latin exorbitare, “to go off the track”: ex- (out of) + orbita (track, rut).

mn.cue: EX-ORBIT: a price blasted OUT OF ORBIT
mn.text: One cupcake for five hundred dollars? The price has rocketed right out of orbit: it is {exorbitant}.

scene.alt: A teen gasps at a cupcake priced at five hundred dollars while a rocket blasts off nearby.

words.def: far greater than is usual or reasonable
words.ex: Pip spends an {inordinate} amount of time choosing his socks.
words.ctx: The project took an {inordinate} amount of time; what should have been a weekend job stretched into four whole months.
words.etym: From Latin inordinatus, “disordered”: in- (not) + ordinare (to put in order).

mn.text: From sunrise to sunset, Grandpa polishes his old car, again and again: he spends an {inordinate} amount of time on it.

scene.alt: A grandfather lovingly polishes his already gleaming car from sunrise to moonrise.

words.def: done without good reason; uncalled for
words.ex: The movie was spoiled by {gratuitous} explosions that had nothing to do with the story.
words.ctx: Her criticism of his essay was fair, but the {gratuitous} remark about his handwriting was simply unkind and added nothing.
words.etym: From Latin gratuitus, “free, done without pay,” from gratia (favor).
words.note: Gratuitous can also mean given free, without charge, its older sense; a gratuity is a tip.

mn.cue: GRATIS = for free: and for NO reason
mn.text: Pip walks by minding his own business, and Rosa calls out “Silly hat!” for no reason at all: the remark is {gratuitous}.

scene.alt: A teen girl points and mocks a boy’s hat for no reason as he walks sadly by.

words.def: an amount that is too much; an excess
words.ex: After the holidays we had a {surfeit} of cookies.
words.ctx: The town suffered not from a lack of parking but from a {surfeit} of it; huge empty lots covered land that could have been parks.
words.etym: From Old French sorfait, “excess,” from sorfaire (to overdo): sor (over) + faire (to do).

mn.text: After the party, Kai and Zoe stare at a mountain of candy, far more than they could ever eat: a {surfeit} of sweets.

scene.alt: Two children face a heap of candy, far more than they can eat; one looks dizzy.

words.def: to flood; to overwhelm with a huge amount
words.ex: After the storm, the swollen river {inundated} the low fields.
words.ctx: When the radio show praised her bakery, Lin was {inundated} with orders, so many that she had to hire three new bakers to keep up.
words.etym: From Latin inundare, “to flood”: in- (onto) + unda (wave).

mn.cue: IN + UNDA (wave): a WAVE of letters rolls IN
mn.text: After the radio show, wave after wave of order letters pours into Lin’s little bakery until she can barely see over them: she is {inundated}.

labels.text: UNDA = WAVE: a flood of letters

scene.alt: A baker is swamped by a wave of order letters pouring into her office.

after.html: gratuitous means uncalled for, but it can also mean free of charge (the same root as gratis and gratuity, a tip). redundant means unneeded because repeated: “free gift,” “past history” and “unexpected surprise” are all redundant.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The phrase “past history” is {redundant}, because all history is past.

after.cap: Saying the same thing twice is redundant.

items.why: Every surprise is unexpected, so “unexpected surprise” says the same thing twice: it is redundant.

items.q: In “The museum offers gratuitous tours on Sundays,” gratuitous means…
items.why: Gratuitous can mean free of charge, from the Latin for a favor. More often it means uncalled for, so read the context.

items.q: True or false: a surplus is an amount left over beyond what is needed.
items.why: True. Sur (over) + plus (more): a surplus is extra.

items.q: Which word best describes a forty-dollar bottle of water?
items.why: A price far too high is exorbitant.
